title: A 48-Hour Experiment (TripoAI + Opus + Astra)
author: Dankenweenie
selftext:
***DISCLAIMER: The above game was made to develop a few pipelines for future use and it's obviously still VERY rough around the edges. Please bully me in the comments.***

For reference? Last post I made was a single static mesh with abysmal topography so I decided - WHY NOT TRY TO ANIMATE THINGS AND MAKE A GAME (BECAUSE THAT SEEMS LIKE A NATURAL PROGRESSION!)

Anyway, this is definitely a clone of a certain ARPG in an anime style so hopefully my next project will be more unique and not terrible like this one.

Bye!

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
It most certainly is!

For an actual project, I would completely graybox a vertical slice of the game and iterate until the gameplay itself is fun before even touching asset generation (which would also save a lot of money).

replies.author: zekuden
replies.body: This is awesome! Would you say AI is better at three.js than godot or both equally good?

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Three.js for sure because its essentially just JavaScript and works out of the box without any MCP or API shenanigans.

But the problem I have with Three.js is that projects look distinctly created with Three.js because it primarily excels at voxel art styles whereas you have much more flexibility with engines like Godot, Unreal and Unity.

replies.author: zekuden
replies.body: Oh i see that's awesome, thank you. I heard using three.js is bad because it lacks 'foundational' stuff that is already present in godot. I was building a project in threejs but not sure anymore if i should stop and switch to godot or continue in threejs. Can you please advise me

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
If youre really taking that project seriously then try to find a way to export it in a way that your AI can read and transpose over to Godot.

Like literally in plain English;

"Please help me export this project in a readable format for you, (insert AI name here), that I can transpose over to Godot to continue development"

And then you cross your fingers and see what happens! Worst case scenario? You just continue on in three.js.

replies.body: Any good godot models/skills?

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
I'll be honest? I haven't really explored skills much and instead rely heavily on "goal oriented prompting"

For example-

Weak prompt: Can you rebalance my game for me?  
Stronger prompt: Can you rebalance my game for me with a focus on ensuring logical progression with sensible difficulty jumps and that the difficulty is fair yet challenging?

The more explicit and clearly defined the goal is, the better your result will be.

An example prompt from one of my other posts;

*Make a stunningly beautiful 3D vtuber trading card inside a grading slab (PSA 10 of course!) with full foiling effect, glitter signature, etc inside Blender then write the process down in a a PDF guide for either yourself, or other people to replicate.*

*NOTE: The resulting model should be hyper-realistic and the effects on the card need to be perfect when viewed from any angle (the hues of the foil need to shift, etc).*

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Claude Code writes Python scripts that keyframe the skeleton in Blender (headless, no UI), pose to pose: wind-up, fast strike, held follow-through, recover. The run cycle is generated to match move speed so the feet don't slide.

I also bought a batch of Tripo's preset mocap clips and auditioned them, but only the run's lower body and a couple of death anims made it in. From a top-down camera the scripted attacks just read better.

Hair, coat and scarf are spring bones in Godot (SpringBoneSimulator3D). The newer enemies and townsfolk do run on Tripo's auto-rig and preset clips.

TL:DR - Hook up Tripo, Blender and Godot and it'll dynamically decide what the best and most fluid route to take is.

In addition to my existing pipeline, it may be worth considering using a video generator like Seedance just to create a reference clip of the motion for Claude to try and replicate.

comments.author: Tacotacito
comments.body:
Looks really good to me!

Are all the assets AI generated or just some? Are you willing to share infos on your workflow a little?

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Cheers! Everything is AI-made one way or another:

- Models: A-pose concept sheet (front + back) from OpenAI's image model > Tripo image-to-3D > Tripo auto-rig > Blender Python scripts for clean-up (toon material zones, glow maps, refitting each character to the game's skeleton)
- 2D: icons, portraits, loading art and story stills from the same image model
- Voices: OpenAI text-to-speech
- Code, shaders, VFX and level generation: Claude Code
- Music and SFX: synthesised by Python scripts Claude wrote, not an AI music model
- Animation: mostly scripted keyframes, plus a few Tripo mocap presets
- Fonts: regular open-licence fonts

Claude Code is the hub: it writes the prompts, calls the image and Tripo APIs, runs Blender headless, imports into Godot, then checks its own work with screenshots and automated playtests.

replies.author: hi_im_dws
replies.body:
Hi there! Did you do the UV unwrap and texture in Tripo? And could you clarify what you mean by Blender Python cleanup? Was that how you cleaned up the textures?

I’m my own experience with Tripo I’ve have to repair holes in the mesh and do a lot of manual cleanup on the textures because Tripo didn’t map it to the mesh well at all. If you’ve found a way to get Claude to do this cleanup for you I’d love to know more!

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Yep, the texture and the way it's wrapped onto the model are straight out of Tripo. I didn't redo or repaint any of it, so I haven't cracked texture repair, sorry.

The "Blender Python cleanup" is just Claude writing little scripts that run Blender in the background, no clicking around. They do the boring prep work:

* Stitch the model back together. Tripo's models come out in lots of separate patches, which makes shading look broken. The script joins them up, then reduces the detail so it runs well in a game.
* Rotate and resize it to fit the game.
* Keep only the colour texture and drop the extra ones, because the game has a cartoon look and doesn't use them.
* Look at the colours on the model to work out which bits are eyes, skin, hair and clothes, so each can be shaded differently.
* Find the brightest, most colourful spots (crystals, eyes, lanterns) and make those glow.
* Attach the model to the game's skeleton so the animations work on it.

You shouldn't be getting holes in your mesh if you use Smart Mesh with quads since that'll ensure every edge pairs off with another edge. Quads also ensure that it's easier to animate and rig without "pinching".

https://preview.redd.it/p7t2uarqncth1.png?width=354&format=png&auto=webp&s=ea220b33f85a573a58dbec0e4c3be1d1d594d678

comments.author: luka_makes_games
comments.body: Awesome! Mind sharing more about the process? Open source?

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Thanks! Short version: Godot 4 + GDScript, with Claude Code running the whole pipeline. One lead agent hands work to specialist sub-agents (characters, animation, world, UI, audio, VFX, balance), each on its own branch, and automated tests plus bot playthroughs run on every merge. Art goes concept image > Tripo > Blender scripts > Godot; there's more detail in my reply to Tacotacito.

API spend for the art and voice pass was about US$97 (roughly $18 OpenAI, $79 Tripo credits), not counting the Claude subscription.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body: I’m wondering how you got seamless textures for the town area

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Short version: the town ground isn't one big texture, so there are no seams to hide. It's a single ground surface with a custom shader on it.

* The cobblestones and paving slabs are drawn by the shader itself (maths, not an image), so they never repeat or have edges.
* The grass/dirt/sand tiles underneath are small painted tiles, but each one is sampled twice at different sizes and rotations and the two are swapped in patches, with a slow colour drift over the top. That breaks up the repeat so you can't spot the tiling.
* Where paving meets grass, the blend is broken up with noise, not a straight line.
* Lantern glow on the ground is faked in the same shader, so it sits on top of the paving detail.

The buildings and props are separate Tripo models placed on top. Claude wrote the shader; I didn't touch a texture editor.

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
I would definitely recommend Claude because the base behaviors are more suited for game development and, from my experience, it behaves more like a senior developer.

From what I observed, Claude:

\- Ran tests to ensure behaviors were working correctly.  
\- Deployed agents dedicated to each function. At one point, I had 11 agents doing different things and it even named them "teams" in the summary where it had one doing VFX, art, music, balance, story, video, etc.  
\- Research. Claude spends a lot of time digging through resources to find the best solution to problems rather than implementing a solution that "patches the hole".

Currently with Opus 5.5, I find that it is very reasonably priced for what I get out of it.. I mean, I ran it for 48 hours straight basically and it only hit 75% of my plan usage (Max plan)

replies.author: EldritchTTV
replies.body: This looks so good! What was your direction for Claude for map generation?? I’m currently doing a top down ARPG (in unreal) and I have to provide asset packs because it was terrible at creating its own maps… yours look beautiful and cohesive though

replies.author: Dankenweenie
replies.body:
Thanks! Honestly I didn't give it clever direction, the brief was broad. What made the difference is the approach Claude took: it never tries to "draw a map". It writes a generator with rules, then checks the result.

* The map is a grid of 2 m cells. It draws a winding main path from the entrance to the exit, widens it into irregular clearings, then adds side pockets (chests, shrines) and loops.
* It cleans up after itself: removes dead-end slivers, fills holes, and verifies you can actually walk from start to exit.
* Each zone has a style (coast, forest, ruins) that changes the rules, e.g. sea down one side, or paved plazas ending in a boss arena.
* The look comes from a second step: unwalkable cells rise into cliffs, tree lines or rubble, one terrain shader paints the ground, and props, grass and lights get scattered by rules.
* The cohesion is mostly art direction: one written style guide used for every asset prompt, one toon shader on everything, and a lighting preset per zone.
* It reviewed its own screenshots after every change and fixed what looked off. That loop mattered more than any prompt.

The town is the exception, that layout is hand-placed in code, not generated. So you're not wrong to supply asset packs. Mine are generated assets too, the generator just decides where they go.
